title: 1 Samuel 15:24–35
context: Saul confesses that he sinned because he feared the people, and asks Samuel to return with him to worship. Samuel refuses, and when Saul grabs his robe and it tears, Samuel declares that the LORD has torn the kingdom from him and given it to a neighbor who is better. He adds that the Strength of Israel will not lie or change his mind, for he is not a man. Samuel then honors Saul before the elders, executes Agag at Gilgal, and departs, mourning Saul for the rest of his life. The section closes by repeating that the LORD grieved that he had made Saul king.

verses.text: Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned; for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul confesses that he sinned because he feared the people and obeyed their voice. Arminian readers note that this admission finally names the real motive, though it comes only after repeated excuses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the confession a recognition of sin that seems focused on consequences and status. Shared ground: Saul’s fear of the people rather than of God lies at the root of his failure, and both traditions read it as a lesson for leaders.

verses.text: Now therefore, please pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul asks Samuel to pardon his sin and return with him to worship. Arminian readers note that he seeks restoration, though the request is directed to Samuel and is tied to his public standing as king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the request seems to seek Samuel’s public presence more than reconciliation with God. Both traditions acknowledge that the sincerity of Saul’s confession is debated, and the text does not settle every question about it.

verses.text: Samuel said to Saul, “I will not return with you; for you have rejected the LORD’s word, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel refuses to return, repeating that Saul rejected the LORD’s word and the LORD rejected him as king. Arminian readers see a consequence that follows from Saul’s choices and that confession at this point does not reverse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repetition as emphasizing the finality of God’s verdict on Saul’s kingship. Shared ground: the rejection concerns Saul’s office as king over Israel, and both traditions read the refusal as confirming that verdict.

verses.text: As Samuel turned around to go away, Saul grabbed the skirt of his robe, and it tore.
verses.arminianNotes: As Samuel turns, Saul grabs his robe and it tears. Arminian readers see a desperate attempt to hold on, both to the prophet and to the kingdom slipping away from him because of his own actions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the torn robe becoming an acted sign, similar to Ahijah’s torn garment in 1 Kings 11:30. Both traditions read the moment as one in which an ordinary accident is turned into a picture of what God has decided.

verses.text: Samuel said to him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today, and has given it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says the LORD has torn the kingdom from Saul and given it to a neighbor who is better. Arminian readers note that the neighbor is unnamed here, though the next chapter reveals David as the one chosen.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purpose moving forward to David even before he is introduced. Shared ground: the torn robe pictures the transfer of the kingdom, and both traditions read the verse as anticipating the anointing in chapter 16.

verses.text: Also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Strength of Israel will not lie or repent, for he is not a man (compare Numbers 23:19). Arminian readers affirm God’s truthfulness and full foreknowledge, while holding that his grief in 15:11 and 15:35 is genuine.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see this verse as the interpretive key for 15:11 and 15:35: God’s purpose does not change. Shared ground: both traditions affirm that God is truthful and unchanging, and that his verdict on Saul’s kingship will not be reversed.
verses.keyContrast: Here the question is how the language of divine regret in 15:11 and 15:35 fits with this verse’s statement that God does not change His mind. Both traditions affirm God’s truthfulness, His exhaustive foreknowledge, and His immutability. Classical Arminian readers generally take the regret as God’s real relational response to Saul’s free disobedience, which He foresaw but did not cause, while His character and purposes stay constant. Reformed readers generally read the regret as anthropopathic language describing God’s unchanging decree unfolding in history; what changes is Saul’s situation, not God’s plan.

verses.text: Then he said, “I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and come back with me, that I may worship the LORD your God.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul confesses again but asks Samuel to honor him before the elders and Israel. Arminian readers see a concern for public honor mixed with confession, showing how Saul’s priorities remain divided at this moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the request for honor reveals what Saul most wants to preserve. Both traditions read the verse as consistent with Saul’s earlier motives, while recognizing that only God knows the full state of his heart.

verses.text: So Samuel went back with Saul; and Saul worshiped the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel returns with Saul, and Saul worships the LORD. Arminian readers note that Samuel shows a measure of kindness, allowing Saul to worship and keep public order while the judgment on his kingship stands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Samuel honoring the office for the moment without reversing the LORD’s decision. Shared ground: the return does not undo the verdict, and both traditions read it as a gracious act that keeps Israel’s worship intact.

verses.text: Then Samuel said, “Bring Agag the king of the Amalekites here to me!” Agag came to him cheerfully. Agag said, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel calls for Agag, who comes cheerfully, thinking death has passed. Arminian readers note the dramatic irony: Agag believes he is safe because Saul spared him, but the prophet now acts on the command Saul ignored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Agag’s false confidence as a picture of mistaken security before God’s judgment. Both traditions note that the meaning of the word rendered “cheerfully” is debated, but the scene’s irony is clear either way.

verses.text: Samuel said, “As your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women!” Then Samuel cut Agag in pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel tells Agag that as his sword made women childless, so will his mother be, and he cuts Agag in pieces before the LORD. Arminian readers state the act plainly and note that it is framed as justice for Agag’s own violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the execution within the unique command concerning Amalek. Shared ground: both traditions see it as a one-time act tied to that judgment, not a model for anyone today. Later, Esther 3:1 calls Haman an Agagite.

verses.text: Then Samuel went to Ramah; and Saul went up to his house to Gibeah of Saul.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel goes to Ramah, and Saul goes home to Gibeah of Saul. Arminian readers note the physical separation that mirrors the broken relationship between the prophet and the king, each returning to his own town.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the parting as marking the end of Samuel’s role as Saul’s adviser in God’s name. Both traditions read the verse as a quiet but significant break, after which Saul will no longer have the prophet’s guidance.

verses.text: Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death, but Samuel mourned for Saul. The LORD grieved that he had made Saul king over Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel does not see Saul again until his death but mourns for him, and the LORD grieves that he made Saul king. Arminian readers see sorrow in both prophet and God; on the divine grief, see the note at 15:29.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the closing statement in light of 15:29, which they take as clarifying how such grief language should be understood. Shared ground: the chapter ends with genuine sorrow over Saul, not with satisfaction at his fall.
